chunks: And Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Safwan, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who bought a sacrificial animal (Udhiyah), and it died or was stolen before he slaughtered it. He said: 'There is no harm, and if he replaces it, that is better. And if he does not buy another, there is no penalty upon him.'

key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: There is no harm / it is permissible
key_terms.لَيْسَ عَلَيْهِ شَيْءٌ: There is no penalty/obligation upon him

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a sacrificial animal dies or is stolen before slaughter?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the fiqh of *daman* (liability) for sacrificial animals (*udhiyah*) prior to slaughter, establishing that the loss is excused (*la ba'sa*) since the animal is not yet consecrated for the specific act of slaughter. The Imam’s distinction between merely replacing the animal and the superior merit of doing so reflects the Shia emphasis on voluntary supererogatory acts (*mustahabb*) in worship. This ruling underscores the principle that financial loss in religious obligations is borne by the owner unless negligence is proven, aligning with the broader juristic consensus on pre-slaughter risks.
